sentences.text: The great auk was the sole modern species within its genus, Pinguinus.
It possessed wings measuring only 15 cm in length, a trait that rendered the bird flightless.
Carl Linnaeus formally described this species as one of 4,400 in his work Systema Naturae.
However, the bird was not placed in its own genus until 1791.
Today, museum collections hold approximately 78 skins, 75 eggs, and 24 complete skeletons.
This species became extinct in 1852.
Great Britain banned the killing of great auks for their feathers in 1794.
The final pair was killed on 3 June 1844 on the island of Eldey.
Its diet included fish such as Atlantic menhaden and capelin, along with crustaceans.
Great auk pairs formed lifelong bonds.
Both parents incubated the egg for about six weeks before hatching.
These birds are believed to have lived approximately 20 to 25 years.
The great auk was closely related to the little auk, also known as the dovekie.
Due to its resemblance to the razorbill, it was often classified in the genus Alca, following Linnaeus.
Some ornithologists still argue that the species should remain in the genus Alca.
It holds the distinction of being the only British bird recorded as extinct in historic times.
Fossil records of the great auk range from the Middle Pleistocene to the Holocene.
The species first appeared around 400,000 years ago.
During the non-breeding season, great auks foraged in the waters of the North Atlantic.
They bred on rocky, remote islands offering easy ocean access and plentiful food.
The origin of the word 'penguin' is debated, with one theory suggesting it derives from the Welsh 'pen gwyn', meaning 'white head'.
It is debated whether great auk bones found in Florida resulted from the species being present there or from aboriginal trading.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources has accepted a claim of a live great auk sighted in 1852 on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland.
There is an ongoing and controversial debate about reviving the great auk using DNA from collected specimens.
